subject: radiology
title: Discovery and Physics of X-rays: Roentgen and Beam Properties

steps.title: Roentgen's Serendipitous Discovery
steps.tx: **Roentgen discovery of X-rays** occurred on the evening of November 8, 1895, at the University of Würzburg. Professor Wilhelm Conrad Roentgen was investigating electrical discharges inside an evacuated Hittorf-Crookes cathode-ray tube wrapped in black cardboard. Across his darkened laboratory, a paper screen coated with barium platinocyanide began fluorescing brightly, revealing invisible, penetrating radiation that he designated X-rays.

steps.title: The First Diagnostic Radiograph
steps.tx: **First human radiograph** was produced on December 22, 1895, when Roentgen exposed the hand of his wife, Anna Bertha Ludwig. The resulting historic image clearly displayed the phalangeal and metacarpal bones alongside the dense silhouette of her gold wedding ring. This groundbreaking proof of non-destructive internal imaging earned Roentgen the inaugural Nobel Prize in Physics in 1901.

steps.tx: One hand with a ring changed medicine in a single winter evening. The **Roentgen hand radiograph** of Anna Bertha showed bone and wedding ring silhouetted by rays that passed through flesh, proving internal imaging without a scalpel was possible. Within months the technique spread to hospitals across the world, faster than most technologies move today. Its grainy bones remain the founding image of an entire specialty and its daily habits of looking inside patients.
steps.say: The first human radiograph showed Anna Bertha Roentgen hand bones and ring in 1895. It founded medical imaging within months worldwide.

steps.title: Fundamental Electromagnetic Characteristics
steps.tx: **Electromagnetic X-ray spectrum** waves travel in straight lines at the speed of light in vacuum, spanning wavelengths from 0.01 to 10 nanometres with frequencies between 30 petahertz and 30 exahertz. Possessing neither electrical charge nor rest mass, X-ray photons cannot be deflected by magnetic or electrical fields. Their energy is calculated as Planck's constant multiplied by frequency.

steps.title: The Inverse Square Law
steps.tx: **Inverse square law calculation** establishes that the intensity of an unattenuated X-ray beam is inversely proportional to the square of the distance from the source. Because photons diverge symmetrically from the focal spot, doubling the distance from 1 metre to 2 metres distributes the identical photon quantity over four times the area, dropping the radiation intensity to exactly one-fourth.

steps.title: Exponential Tissue Attenuation
steps.tx: **Exponential attenuation coefficient** values dictate how X-ray beams weaken as they traverse matter, governed by the Beer-Lambert law: intensity equals initial intensity multiplied by e to the power of negative linear attenuation coefficient times thickness. The linear attenuation coefficient reflects the combined probabilities of photoelectric absorption and Compton scattering per centimetre of specific human tissue.

left.title: Linear Attenuation Coefficient (u)
points: Fraction of photons attenuated per unit length (cm-1)
Varies directly with physical tissue density
Dependent on tissue physical state (ice vs water vs steam)

right.title: Mass Attenuation Coefficient (u/p)
points: Independent of physical state or density packing
Reflected by atomic composition and photon energy

steps.title: Five Basic Radiographic Densities
steps.tx: **Five radiographic densities** form the foundation of plain film interpretation, categorized by their distinct degree of photon absorption. Air or gas absorbs the fewest photons and appears dark black. Fat appears dark grey. Fluid, blood, and soft tissue muscle appear medium grey. Bone and calcium absorb substantial photons, appearing bright white, while metal appears intensely opaque radiopaque white.

steps.title: Compton Scattering Interactions
steps.tx: **Compton scattering interaction** dominates at photon energies above 30 kiloelectron volts in soft tissues. An incident photon collides with a loosely bound outer-shell electron, ejecting the electron and deflecting the photon with reduced energy at an oblique angle. Compton scatter accounts for nearly all secondary radiation striking staff members and produces diffuse radiographic fog that degrades image contrast.

steps.title: Photoelectric Effect and Contrast
steps.tx: **Photoelectric effect absorption** occurs when an incoming photon completely transfers its energy to an inner-shell electron, ejecting it as a photoelectron. Because the probability of photoelectric interaction is proportional to the atomic number cubed divided by photon energy cubed, dense osseous structures with effective atomic number 13.8 absorb far more photons than soft tissue with atomic number 7.4.

left.title: Photoelectric Absorption
points: Complete photon absorption by inner orbital electron
Proportional to Z cubed divided by energy cubed

right.title: Compton Scattering
points: Partial energy transfer to outer orbital electron
Independent of atomic number; depends on electron density
